title: Image capture and pre-filtering for 3D photogrammetry of coral colonies
author: Wyatt C Million
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bgdcjs2w

steps.title: Gather Materials and Supplies
steps.instruction: Collect all components: four HDPE bars (9.75" × 1.25" × 0.25"), three 0.25" stainless‑steel carriage bolts (1 in long), three 0.25" stainless‑steel washers, three 0.25" stainless‑steel wing nuts, electrical tape or glue, small dive weights (optional), waterproof printable paper, and a CoralWatch Coral Health Chart color reference card. The HDPE sheets should be 1/4" thick (source: usplastic.com). Estimated material cost is about $12.

steps.title: Drill and Prepare HDPE Bars
steps.instruction: On each of the four HDPE bars, drill two centered holes 7/8" from each end using a 1/4" drill bit. Square off the backside of each hole to create a pocket approximately 1/8" deep with a chisel or flat‑head screwdriver; this pocket will hold the carriage bolt head and prevent rotation when the wing nut is tightened.

steps.title: Assemble Tomahawk Frame
steps.instruction: Overlay the bars to form a rectangular (or square) frame. Insert a carriage bolt through the overlapping holes of adjacent bars, add a washer on the far side, and secure with a wing nut. Loosen the wing nuts to allow the bars to pivot and adjust the frame to the size and shape of the coral to be photographed; retighten the wing nuts to lock the frame in place. Attach small dive weights to the back or corners if wave energy is high.

steps.title: Print and Cut Metashape Markers
steps.instruction: Open Agisoft Metashape on a desktop, go to Tools > Markers > Print Markers, and select a target size appropriate for the coral (e.g., 2 mm). Choose to print twenty 12‑bit, 2 mm markers per page. Print directly onto waterproof printable paper, ensuring the paper will not melt in the printer. Rearrange the PDF layout if needed to increase marker density (see PStargets2mm_dense.pdf). Cut the markers out with scissors.

steps.title: Attach Markers and Color Card to Tomahawk
steps.instruction: Using electrical tape (preferred for easy replacement) or glue, affix the cut Metashape markers onto the faces of the Tomahawk so they are visible from all viewing angles. Also cut the four scales from the CoralWatch Coral Health Chart and attach one scale to each Tomahawk face with tape or glue, ensuring the colored sections remain visible.

steps.title: Prepare Camera Settings
steps.instruction: Use an Olympus TG‑Tough 4 or 5 model. Set the camera to manual shutter release (press the shutter button for each shot), enable underwater mode, and select an appropriate white‑balance preset or custom white balance to reduce blue/green tint. Disable zoom, and keep the camera orientation constant (do not switch between landscape and portrait). Optionally, interval mode can be used but may be slow; burst mode is fast but may produce excess images.

steps.title: Practice Scaling and Photo Capture
steps.instruction: Before diving, practice on dead coral skeletons or sticks to confirm that the Tomahawk remains stable and that clear photos can be obtained. Ensure the scaling object (Tomahawk) does not move during a photo series; if it does, restart the series. If wave energy is high, place a dive weight on top of the Tomahawk.

steps.title: Capture Multi‑Angle Photo Set
steps.instruction: Position the camera 5–10 inches away from the coral with the lens parallel to the substrate (0° angle) and rotate around the coral, taking overlapping photos (~80% overlap). Then move to a 45° angle off the substrate, keep the camera 5–10 inches away, and rotate again. For complex branch intersections, move 3–6 inches from the coral and capture additional close‑up photos. Finally, take 1–2 top‑down photos that include both the coral and the entire Tomahawk scaling object. Avoid casting shadows, keep the arm moving rather than the body, and include a reference shot of the sky or your hand when restarting a new coral series.

steps.title: Organize and Filter Photos
steps.instruction: On the computer, create a separate photoset folder for each coral colony. Within each set, delete blurry, out‑of‑focus, or coral‑absent images to speed up later Metashape processing.

steps.title: Batch Color‑Correct in Lightroom
steps.instruction: Open Adobe Lightroom, add photos via the + icon or File > Add Photos, and enable “Review” for import. Select one representative image, adjust Exposure, Contrast, Sharpening, and White Balance to make the coral stand out from the background. Copy the edit settings (Photo > Copy Edit Settings) and paste them onto the remaining images in the set (Photo > Paste Edit Settings). Verify the batch‑edited images, then save all files (File > Save to).

steps.title: Generate 3D Model with Metashape
steps.instruction: Import the organized, color‑corrected photo set into Agisoft Metashape. Use the printed markers (now attached to the Tomahawk) for scaling and alignment. Run the standard workflow (Align Photos, Build Dense Cloud, Build Mesh, Build Texture). For large datasets, consider using the provided command‑line scripts on a high‑performance computing system (see https://github.com/wyattmillion/Coral3DPhotogram).

description: Overview Creating 3D models from 2D images requires collecting photos of your subject from numerous angles so that the software can use overlap from those photos to recreate the dimensions of your subject. So in general, more photos with a lot of overlap between photos is better. We recommend 80% overlap between photos to ensure that Agisoft Metashape can accurately generate the coral model. The number of photos is dependent on the size and complexity of the coral. When in doubt, err in favor of more photos. Here are the number of photos we typically take for Acropora cervicornis colonies of varying sizes: 5-20 cm TLE : 40 -75 photos 15 - 40 cm TLE: 75 - 125 photos 40-70 cm TLE: 125 - 175 photos 90-125 cm TLE: 175 - 300 photos An 8 cm TLE coral that required 52 photos A 29 cm TLE coral that required 97 photos A 60 cm TLE coral that required 143 photos A 114 cm TLE coral that required 276 photos
